text:
Quinton Byfield is 24, and Los Angeles has handed him a bigger job. He's on the ice for 81% of the Kings' power-play chances, up from 44% last season, and his own chance quality has jumped to 1.24 expected goals per 60 minutes from 0.82 (expected goals measure the quality of chances). That's what a breakout usually looks like before the points arrive.

The points haven't arrived. He has 7 in 16 games, fewer per game than last season, and the gap looks like bad luck more than bad play. The Kings have scored 10.1 fewer goals than their chances deserve with him on the ice, and at five-on-five they take about 55% of the expected goals when he's out there, more than 6 points better than without him. That usually swings back.

Evolving-Hockey had him driving play at the 90th percentile among forwards last season and drawing more penalties than he takes. Corey Sznajder's All Three Zones tracking had 62% of his exits leaving the zone with possession. Sixteen games is a small sample, and the Kings have lost four straight. Watch whether his on-ice goals catch up to the chances; his role says they should.
headline: Byfield's role grew faster than his points
